prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength and interrogated together, bringing frequency standards to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B012 (Katori, Ye) as a single prize part. Seven of eight members reach it from different directions, and the reasons are scientific rather than numerical: one original idea (state-independent trapping of thousands of atoms at a magic wavelength), an instrument whose quoted 10^-18 uncertainty is measured and checked in independent comparisons across several national laboratories, and applications already in use (relativistic geodesy, tests of constants). As an instrumentalist I value that the claim is a number others can check, and that the check has been done. The citation should be worded around the lattice and many-atom interrogation, not around accuracy in general, so it is plainly distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single ions. I do not see a need for a second part: no alternative offers a cleaner allocation under the three-person cap.
statement.case_against: The credit history is the genuine weakness. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the strontium versus ytterbium first-demonstration sequence, are not covered by two names, and neither I nor, by their own statements, several colleagues can verify that history from the supplied material. Ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty, as Johansson notes, so the citation cannot rest on accuracy alone. B042 has the larger recent footprint in the field, and Eriksson is right that a conceptual advance is a different kind of achievement from an instrument; the committee should state openly that it is choosing an instrument achievement this year.

responses.point: Prefers B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the most defensible condensed-matter common ground, treats the pending redefinition of the second as leaving the impact of B012 unfinished, and lists B012 only as an alternative.
responses.response: I take B030 seriously: the Z2 invariant is a real concept and the HgTe observation is decisive. But you yourself state the problem: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the prediction Molenkamp tested, and the three-dimensional work are outside the three names, and the 2016 prize covered topological phases. That gap is larger than anything attached to B012, where the main question is early-demonstration history rather than a missing prediction. On the redefinition, the 10^-18 performance exists and has been reproduced independently, and a prize for a measured achievement should not wait for a metrology conference decision. On novelty, a citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation separates the work from 2005 and 2012. I have not changed my view because of your file, but I would accept B030 as a later-year candidate if the committee can settle its credit.

responses.point: Asks that the citation not rest on accuracy in general because ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty, and notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes narrow the room for another precision-measurement award; moved from B005 to B012 and records a WACQT conflict.
responses.response: Your point on ion clocks changes my wording. My round-1 citation led with the 10^-18 figure, which is shared with ion clocks, so I now lead with the lattice itself and many atoms interrogated together, with accuracy as the consequence. On room after 2005 and 2012, I would say the new achievement counts if it is a distinct idea, and the lattice is. I note your conflict disclosure and agree it is right that B005 stays out of the preferred configuration, which in any case I would not support this year after the 2025 prize.

responses.point: Holds B012 first, says the committee should not wait on a regulatory step, accepts B042 as lead if the committee judges the field mature, and would not put B030 in a preferred configuration because of the BHZ gap.
responses.response: I agree on timing and on B030. On B042, my round-1 statement conceded more on maturity and credit than I would defend as a lead position, so I record the same view as yours: the 2018 experiments are eight years old, the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, and credit is split among Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Efetov and the early band-flattening theorists, so a three-name allocation including Bistritzer is not secure. These are matters of maturity, not merit, and I would put B042 first in a later year if the mechanism and credit settle.

responses.point: Moved from B028 to B012 but asks that the overlap with earlier clock work be checked against the history, and thinks the omissions may make a two-name prize unfair.
responses.response: The overlap and the omissions are the right test, and I think they can be partly answered. The lattice idea and its first realisation are Katori's, and Ye's group took accuracy, coherence and comparisons to the 10^-18 level; Hall and Haensch in 2005 and Wineland in 2012 honoured the comb and single-ion control, which this work uses but does not duplicate. What I cannot confirm is how the first Sr and Yb demonstrations divide, and I would ask that the committee note this limit in the record rather than treat it as settled. If that history were found to give a third person a decisive share, I would revisit the names, not the part.

uncertainties: The first-demonstration and credit history of lattice clocks (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke, the Sr and Yb groups, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) cannot be verified from the supplied material, so a two-name allocation rests on the attribution I and others accept.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; I think it is, but this depends on the citation wording.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second ought to be a maturity condition; I do not think so, but Eriksson does.
Whether B042 will be more compelling in one or two years if the superconducting mechanism and credit settle.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my documented work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle physics) has no recorded connection to the lattice-clock, twisted-graphene or topological-insulator candidates or their credited names. I am Chair and will not favour any field; I note that I changed my preferred part between the opening and round 1, and I give my reasons above rather than rely on the count of supporters.
